claim: PV-expressing interneurons were identified in hippocampal CA1 (n = 56 cells in 45 mice) using short-latency, low-jitter responses to blue light in PV-Cre/ChR2 mice.
source: During the baseline period, we identified PV- (n = 56 cells in 45 mice) and SST- (n = 42 cells in 34 mice) expressing interneurons in PV-Cre/ChR2 or SST-Cre/ChR2 mice, respectively, by their short-latency, low-jitter responses to blue light (Figure 1B; see Materials and methods) (Cardin et al., 2009; Lima et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from optogenetic identification of PV interneurons, with specific cell counts and mouse numbers.

claim: SST-expressing interneurons were identified in hippocampal CA1 (n = 42 cells in 34 mice) using short-latency, low-jitter responses to blue light in SST-Cre/ChR2 mice.
source: During the baseline period, we identified PV- (n = 56 cells in 45 mice) and SST- (n = 42 cells in 34 mice) expressing interneurons in PV-Cre/ChR2 or SST-Cre/ChR2 mice, respectively, by their short-latency, low-jitter responses to blue light (Figure 1B; see Materials and methods) (Cardin et al., 2009; Lima et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from optogenetic identification of SST interneurons, with specific cell counts and mouse numbers.

claim: PV cells displayed narrow spike waveforms on average.
source: On average, PV cells displayed narrow spike waveforms, whereas SST cells exhibited broader waveforms (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations of spike waveform characteristics with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: SST cells exhibited broader spike waveforms on average.
source: On average, PV cells displayed narrow spike waveforms, whereas SST cells exhibited broader waveforms (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations of spike waveform characteristics with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: There was extensive overlap of waveform characteristics among PV and SST populations.
source: However, there was extensive overlap of waveform characteristics among the populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B), indicating that spike waveform alone is not sufficient to distinguish cell types under these conditions.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations of waveform overlap with reference to figures.

claim: Spike waveform alone is not sufficient to distinguish PV and SST cell types under these experimental conditions.
source: However, there was extensive overlap of waveform characteristics among the populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B), indicating that spike waveform alone is not sufficient to distinguish cell types under these conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed overlap in waveform characteristics.

claim: The two identified interneuron populations (PV and SST) were largely non-overlapping within CA1.
source: Histological analysis confirmed that the two identified interneuron populations were largely non-overlapping within CA1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-K).
evidence: The manuscript reports histological data confirming the separation of the two populations.

claim: Unidentified cells (n = 49 cells in 26 mice) were simultaneously recorded along with ChR2-tagged units in PV-Cre and SST-Cre mice or in the pyramidal cell layer of wild-type mice.
source: In some experiments, unidentified cells (n = 49 cells in 26 mice) were simultaneously recorded along with ChR2-tagged units in PV-Cre and SST-Cre mice or in the pyramidal cell layer of wild-type mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data on recordings of unidentified cells.

claim: A subset of unidentified cells (n = 26 cells in 16 mice) were regular spiking (RS), putative excitatory cells with characteristic broad spike waveforms and relatively low baseline firing rates.
source: A subset of these unidentified cells (n = 26 cells in 16 mice) were regular spiking (RS), putative excitatory cells with characteristic broad spike waveforms and relatively low baseline firing rates (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental characterization of RS cells based on their electrophysiological properties.

claim: Most PV cells strongly increased their firing rate in the last preictal period compared to the first (94.4%, p<0.001).
source: Strikingly, we found that most PV cells strongly increased their firing rate in the last preictal period as compared to the first (94.4%, p<0.001, Binomial test) or third (83.3%, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data on PV cell firing rates.

claim: 83.3% of PV cells strongly increased their firing rate in the last preictal period compared to the third (p<0.001).
source: Strikingly, we found that most PV cells strongly increased their firing rate in the last preictal period as compared to the first (94.4%, p<0.001, Binomial test) or third (83.3%, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data on PV cell firing rates.

claim: The sharp, late increase in firing rate observed in PV cells was not observed in SST or RS cells.
source: In contrast, this sharp, late increase in firing rate was not observed in SST or RS cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative experimental observations across cell types.

claim: Increased firing of PV, SST, and RS cells was independent of the latency to ictal onset.
source: Increased firing of PV, SST, and RS cells was independent of the latency to ictal onset (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-E) and was observed in the absence of significant changes in spike waveform amplitude over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of experimental data showing independence from seizure latency.

claim: Increased firing of PV, SST, and RS cells was observed in the absence of significant changes in spike waveform amplitude over time.
source: Increased firing of PV, SST, and RS cells was independent of the latency to ictal onset (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-E) and was observed in the absence of significant changes in spike waveform amplitude over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of experimental data on spike waveform amplitude.

claim: There was no difference in the preictal trajectory of FS and non-FS PV interneurons.
source: There was no difference in the preictal trajectory of FS and non-FS PV interneurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative analysis of experimental data on PV interneuron subtypes.

claim: A similar increase in PV cell firing rates during the late preictal period was observed in acute Pilocarpine-induced seizures.
source: We observed a similar increase in PV cell firing rates during the late preictal period preceding Pilocarpine-induced seizures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G-J), suggesting that this is not a unique feature of PTZ-induced seizures.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from a different seizure model showing similar results.

claim: The late preictal increase in PV cell firing is not a unique feature of PTZ-induced seizures.
source: We observed a similar increase in PV cell firing rates during the late preictal period preceding Pilocarpine-induced seizures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G-J), suggesting that this is not a unique feature of PTZ-induced seizures.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observing similar patterns in two different seizure models.

claim: In awake head-fixed mice, PV interneurons showed a sharp increase in firing rate immediately prior to seizure onset.
source: However, only PV interneurons showed a sharp increase in firing rate immediately prior to seizure onset (Figure 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from awake animals showing PV-specific firing rate changes.

claim: After ictal onset, PV firing decreased from the preictal peak back to baseline levels.
source: We found that after ictal onset, PV and SST firing decreased from the preictal peak back to baseline levels (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data on PV cell firing during the ictal period.

claim: After ictal onset, SST firing decreased from the preictal peak back to baseline levels.
source: We found that after ictal onset, PV and SST firing decreased from the preictal peak back to baseline levels (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data on SST cell firing during the ictal period.

claim: RS cells continued to fire at elevated rates during the early ictal period.
source: In contrast, RS cells continued to fire at elevated rates (Figure 2D), suggesting a sustained early ictal increase in the activity of excitatory, but not inhibitory, neurons.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data on RS cell firing during the ictal period.

claim: There is a sustained early ictal increase in the activity of excitatory, but not inhibitory, neurons.
source: In contrast, RS cells continued to fire at elevated rates (Figure 2D), suggesting a sustained early ictal increase in the activity of excitatory, but not inhibitory, neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential firing patterns of RS cells versus PV and SST cells during the ictal period.

claim: During baseline activity, the firing rate of RS cells decreased following ChR2-evoked PV cell spiking.
source: During baseline activity, we found that the firing rate of RS cells decreased following ChR2-evoked PV and SST cell spiking (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data on optogenetically-evoked inhibition of RS cells.

claim: During baseline activity, the firing rate of RS cells decreased following ChR2-evoked SST cell spiking.
source: During baseline activity, we found that the firing rate of RS cells decreased following ChR2-evoked PV and SST cell spiking (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data on optogenetically-evoked inhibition of RS cells.

claim: RS firing suppression by PV cells was not significantly changed across the preictal and early ictal periods as compared to baseline.
source: RS firing suppression was not significantly changed across the preictal and early ictal periods as compared to baseline when the PV cells were driven by optogenetic stimulation (see Materials and methods; Figure 3C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data on optogenetically-evoked inhibition across time periods.

claim: RS suppression by SST cell spiking was maintained throughout preictal and early ictal periods.
source: RS suppression by SST cell spiking was likewise maintained throughout preictal and early ictal periods.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data on optogenetically-evoked inhibition across time periods.

claim: RS suppression in response to PV spiking was consistently observed during the preictal period of awake seizure initiation.
source: However, RS suppression in response to PV and SST spiking was consistently observed during the preictal period of awake seizure initiation (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from awake animals on optogenetically-evoked inhibition.

claim: RS suppression in response to SST spiking was consistently observed during the preictal period of awake seizure initiation.
source: However, RS suppression in response to PV and SST spiking was consistently observed during the preictal period of awake seizure initiation (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from awake animals on optogenetically-evoked inhibition.

claim: Immediately preceding ictal onset in both anesthetized and awake animals, PV cell firing became significantly more regular (less bursty).
source: Immediately preceding ictal onset in both anesthetized and awake animals, PV, but not SST or RS, cell firing became significantly more regular (i.e., less bursty) (Figure 4A–B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data on firing pattern regularity.

claim: SST cell firing did not become significantly more regular immediately preceding ictal onset.
source: Immediately preceding ictal onset in both anesthetized and awake animals, PV, but not SST or RS, cell firing became significantly more regular (i.e., less bursty) (Figure 4A–B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data on firing pattern regularity.

claim: RS cell firing did not become significantly more regular immediately preceding ictal onset.
source: Immediately preceding ictal onset in both anesthetized and awake animals, PV, but not SST or RS, cell firing became significantly more regular (i.e., less bursty) (Figure 4A–B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data on firing pattern regularity.

claim: PV cells showed an increased tendency to fire spikes separated by short (<10 ms) inter-spike-intervals.
source: In addition, PV cells showed an increased tendency to fire spikes separated by short (<10 ms) inter-spike-intervals (ISI; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of experimental data on inter-spike interval statistics.

claim: Unidentified cells with narrow spikes did not exhibit changes in firing rate, firing regularity, or ISI statistics.
source: Unidentified cells with narrow spikes did not exhibit changes in firing rate, firing regularity, or ISI statistics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of experimental data on unidentified narrow-spiking cells.

claim: PV cells showed a peak in spike-field coherence in the 20-28 Hz frequency band that decreased significantly during the preictal period.
source: PV cells showed a peak in SFC in the 20 – 28 Hz frequency band that decreased significantly during the preictal period (Figure 4C–D) in the absence of any loss in LFP power or changes in SFC in the theta or high gamma bands, other prominent hippocampal rhythms associated with interneuron activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of experimental data on spike-field coherence.

claim: The decrease in PV cell spike-field coherence in the 20-28 Hz band occurred in the absence of any loss in LFP power in that band.
source: PV cells showed a peak in SFC in the 20 – 28 Hz frequency band that decreased significantly during the preictal period (Figure 4C–D) in the absence of any loss in LFP power or changes in SFC in the theta or high gamma bands, other prominent hippocampal rhythms associated with interneuron activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of experimental data on LFP power.

claim: PV cells did not show changes in spike-field coherence in the theta or high gamma bands during the preictal period.
source: PV cells showed a peak in SFC in the 20 – 28 Hz frequency band that decreased significantly during the preictal period (Figure 4C–D) in the absence of any loss in LFP power or changes in SFC in the theta or high gamma bands, other prominent hippocampal rhythms associated with interneuron activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of experimental data on spike-field coherence in different frequency bands.

claim: Neither SST nor RS cells showed a change in spike-field coherence across the preictal periods.
source: In contrast, neither SST nor RS cells showed a change in SFC across the preictal periods, suggesting a specific decoupling of PV cells from their normal temporal relationship with the local hippocampal network during the onset of ictal activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of experimental data on spike-field coherence for different cell types.

claim: There is a specific decoupling of PV cells from their normal temporal relationship with the local hippocampal network during the onset of ictal activity.
source: In contrast, neither SST nor RS cells showed a change in SFC across the preictal periods, suggesting a specific decoupling of PV cells from their normal temporal relationship with the local hippocampal network during the onset of ictal activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential changes in spike-field coherence across cell types.

claim: PV cells showed no progressive change in spike probability in response to optogenetic stimulation over the preictal period.
source: PV cells showed no progressive change in spike probability over the preictal period (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of experimental data on optogenetically-evoked responses.

claim: SST cells showed an increase in the slope of their response curve to optogenetic stimulation across the preictal periods.
source: In contrast, SST cells showed an increase in the slope of their response curve and a decrease in their maximal response probability (Rmax) across the preictal periods.
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of experimental data on optogenetically-evoked responses.

claim: SST cells showed a decrease in their maximal response probability (Rmax) to optogenetic stimulation across the preictal periods.
source: In contrast, SST cells showed an increase in the slope of their response curve and a decrease in their maximal response probability (Rmax) across the preictal periods.
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of experimental data on optogenetically-evoked responses.

claim: Changes in interneuron sensitivity to input were not affected by seizure latency.
source: Changes in interneuron sensitivity to input were not affected by seizure latency (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of experimental data showing independence from seizure latency.

claim: There is a progressive preictal attenuation of the response of SST cells to input, potentially limiting their recruitment by network inputs.
source: Together, these data suggest a progressive preictal attenuation of the response of SST cells to input, potentially limiting their recruitment by network inputs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed changes in SST cell response properties.

claim: Synaptic inhibition from PV interneurons remained intact throughout the preictal period and early ictal phase.
source: Surprisingly, synaptic inhibition from parvalbumin- (PV) and somatostatin-expressing (SST) interneurons remained intact throughout the preictal period and early ictal phase.

claim: Synaptic inhibition from SST interneurons remained intact throughout the preictal period and early ictal phase.

evidence: The manuscript reports experimental findings on the maintenance of synaptic inhibition.

claim: PV and SST interneurons exhibited cell-type-specific differences in their preictal firing patterns.
source: However, these two sources of inhibition exhibited cell-type-specific differences in their preictal firing patterns and sensitivity to input.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental findings on differential firing patterns between cell types.

claim: PV and SST interneurons exhibited cell-type-specific differences in their sensitivity to input.
source: However, these two sources of inhibition exhibited cell-type-specific differences in their preictal firing patterns and sensitivity to input.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental findings on differential input sensitivity between cell types.

claim: The onset of ictal activity is not associated with loss of firing by PV and SST interneurons.
source: Our findings suggest that the onset of ictal activity is not associated with loss of firing by these interneurons or a failure of synaptic inhibition but is instead linked with disruptions of the respective roles these interneurons play in the hippocampal circuit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings on interneuron firing and inhibition.

claim: The onset of ictal activity is not associated with a failure of synaptic inhibition from PV and SST interneurons.
source: Our findings suggest that the onset of ictal activity is not associated with loss of firing by these interneurons or a failure of synaptic inhibition but is instead linked with disruptions of the respective roles these interneurons play in the hippocampal circuit.

claim: The onset of ictal activity is linked with disruptions of the respective roles PV and SST interneurons play in the hippocampal circuit.

source: Acute blockade of GABA receptors rapidly initiates seizure activity (Rose and Blakemore, 1974; Treiman, 2001), suggesting the necessity of synaptic inhibition to maintain healthy activity patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Synaptic inhibition is necessary to maintain healthy activity patterns.
source: Acute blockade of GABA receptors rapidly initiates seizure activity (Rose and Blakemore, 1974; Treiman, 2001), suggesting the necessity of synaptic inhibition to maintain healthy activity patterns.

claim: Developmental dysregulation of inhibitory interneurons causes chronic epileptic disorders.
source: Developmental dysregulation of inhibitory interneurons causes chronic epileptic disorders (Lau et al., 2000; Cobos et al., 2005; Rossignol et al., 2013; Tai et al., 2014), and interneurons also appear to be particularly sensitive to seizure-related damage (Sloviter, 1987; de Lanerolle et al., 1989; Robbins et al., 1991; Rice et al., 1996; Gibbs et al., 1997; Cossart et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Interneurons appear to be particularly sensitive to seizure-related damage.
source: Developmental dysregulation of inhibitory interneurons causes chronic epileptic disorders (Lau et al., 2000; Cobos et al., 2005; Rossignol et al., 2013; Tai et al., 2014), and interneurons also appear to be particularly sensitive to seizure-related damage (Sloviter, 1987; de Lanerolle et al., 1989; Robbins et al., 1991; Rice et al., 1996; Gibbs et al., 1997; Cossart et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent work using population imaging in cortex largely observed increased interneuron activity following seizure onset.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

source: Putative fast-spiking interneurons in human cortex may also exhibit increased preictal firing rates (Truccolo et al., 2011).

claim: Previous work has largely found increased preictal firing of putative excitatory hippocampal neurons.
source: In comparison, previous work has largely found increased preictal firing of putative excitatory hippocampal neurons (Cymerblit-Sabba and Schiller, 2010; Jiruska et al., 2010; Fujita et al., 2014), but several reports have highlighted mixed populations, with some neurons increasing and some decreasing firing prior to seizure (Bower and Buckmaster, 2008; Toyoda et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Several reports have highlighted mixed populations of hippocampal neurons, with some increasing and some decreasing firing prior to seizure.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

source: Neocortical GABAergic interneurons exhibit a wide variety of morphologies, molecular markers, and activity patterns, and make synapses on different subcellular domains of target pyramidal cells (Rudy et al., 2011).

claim: GABAergic interneurons make synapses on different subcellular domains of target pyramidal cells.
source: Neocortical GABAergic interneurons exhibit a wide variety of morphologies, molecular markers, and activity patterns, and make synapses on different subcellular domains of target pyramidal cells (Rudy et al., 2011).

source: In the hippocampus, these include the soma-targeting, axo-axonic and basket cells that co-express the calcium binding protein parvalbumin (PV) and the dendrite-targeting O-LM and bistratified interneurons that co-express the peptide somatostatin (SST) (Buhl et al., 1994; Sik et al., 1995; Klausberger et al., 2003; Petilla Interneuron Nomenclature Group et al., 2008; Lapray et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the hippocampus, dendrite-targeting O-LM and bistratified interneurons co-express the peptide somatostatin (SST).
source: In the hippocampus, these include the soma-targeting, axo-axonic and basket cells that co-express the calcium binding protein parvalbumin (PV) and the dendrite-targeting O-LM and bistratified interneurons that co-express the peptide somatostatin (SST) (Buhl et al., 1994; Sik et al., 1995; Klausberger et al., 2003; Petilla Interneuron Nomenclature Group et al., 2008; Lapray et al., 2012).

source: Chemoconvulsant models are reliable and consistent across animals and provide a window into the transition from healthy to pathological neural activity, separating interneuron activity and inhibitory influence in the initial transition to ictal activity from alterations in interneuron activity that are known to occur as a result of seizure-induced cell death or sprouting.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the experimental model used.

claim: Chemoconvulsant models provide a window into the transition from healthy to pathological neural activity.
source: Chemoconvulsant models are reliable and consistent across animals and provide a window into the transition from healthy to pathological neural activity, separating interneuron activity and inhibitory influence in the initial transition to ictal activity from alterations in interneuron activity that are known to occur as a result of seizure-induced cell death or sprouting.

claim: The inhibitory influence of SST interneuron firing on nearby neurons remains largely intact throughout the preictal and early ictal periods.
source: The inhibitory influence of PV and SST interneuron firing on nearby neurons remains largely intact throughout the preictal and early ictal periods, suggesting that seizure activity does not arise from a failure of GABAergic inhibition from these cells.

claim: Seizure activity does not arise from a failure of GABAergic inhibition from PV and SST cells.

claim: Fast-spiking, PV-expressing interneurons are coupled to both high-frequency and theta rhythms in the hippocampus.
source: Fast-spiking, PV-expressing interneurons are coupled to both high-frequency and theta rhythms in the hippocampus, and are thought to contribute to maintaining the fine temporal organization of excitatory-inhibitory interactions (Buzsáki et al., 2003; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Klausberger et al., 2003; Diba et al., 2014; Amilhon et al., 2015; Forro et al., 2015; Huh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PV-expressing interneurons are thought to contribute to maintaining the fine temporal organization of excitatory-inhibitory interactions.
source: Fast-spiking, PV-expressing interneurons are coupled to both high-frequency and theta rhythms in the hippocampus, and are thought to contribute to maintaining the fine temporal organization of excitatory-inhibitory interactions (Buzsáki et al., 2003; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Klausberger et al., 2003; Diba et al., 2014; Amilhon et al., 2015; Forro et al., 2015; Huh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The earliest preictal change observed was a loss of the strong spike-field coherence of PV cell spiking to a prominent low-gamma band.
source: The earliest preictal change we observed was a loss of the strong spike-field coherence of PV cell spiking to a prominent low-gamma band previously observed in mouse hippocampus (Chen et al., 2011; Cabral et al., 2014; Sauer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental findings with citations to previous work on the low-gamma band.

claim: Late preictal increases in PV interneuron firing could lead to irregular firing patterns or bursts in excitatory neurons.
source: Late preictal increases in PV interneuron firing could lead to irregular firing patterns or bursts in excitatory neurons, potentially resulting in hyper-synchronized, pathological entrainment of excitatory activity (Shiri et al., 2015; Yekhlef et al., 2015; Avoli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Late preictal increases in PV interneuron firing could potentially result in hyper-synchronized, pathological entrainment of excitatory activity.

evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: OLM cells innervate the distal tuft dendrites of local excitatory pyramidal neurons, providing potent recurrent feedback within the local circuit.
